source.title: BrainGPT: Unleashing the Potential of EEG Generalist Foundation Model by Autoregressive Pre-training
source.authors: Tong-Tian Yue; Xuan-Ge Gao; Shu-Ning Xue; Ye-Peng Tang; Long-Teng Guo; Jie Jiang; Jing Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some plotted results are flattened into the text, so individual figure values are not reliably recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling trends in EEG autoregressive pre-training, a different modality from the text language-model setting, and reports downstream performance across model and data scales.
record.gate_note: The paper reports EEG reconstruction-loss curves across four model sizes and downstream-task scores across model and pre-training-data sizes. It does not report fitted power-law exponents or prediction errors from extrapolating smaller runs. Values shown only in figures are recorded as figure only. The 12-dataset results in Table IV are not exhaustively extracted; the aggregate scaling result and the EDF exception are included.
record.test_reason: The study varies EEG autoregressive pre-training model size (1.46M to 1.09B) and pre-training tokens (0 to 1B). It reports whether reconstruction loss and downstream accuracy improve with scale. It fits no power law and tests no extrapolation or compute allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim to 'validate the scaling laws' for data and model size in EEG autoregressive pre-training. Their basis: larger models reach lower converged loss, and downstream accuracy rises with model size and pre-training data, with diminishing returns for data. They fit no power law and call the trends preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: EEG electrode-wise autoregressive reconstruction uses MSE by default rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy; the paper varies model size and data volume but does not fit loss laws or test fixed-compute allocation. The objective is an EEG modality extension.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream performance gains from more pre-training data are described as initially substantial and then tapering. EDF accuracy does not increase from Huge to Giant.
record.problems: The scaling experiments are described as preliminary. The paper reports no fitted exponents, extrapolation test, or held-out cross-entropy results. Model-size loss curves are not numerically tabulated, and the data-volume experiment reports downstream performance rather than loss. The pre-training-data comparison uses one stated shuffled token pool and the paper does not vary compute budget.
record.rows_left_out: The per-model, per-dataset downstream results in Table IV are not fully extracted; the average scale trend from Fig. 4(b), the data-volume results from Fig. 5, and the non-monotonic EDF result from Table IV are retained. Other Table IV task/model cells are omitted to stay focused on the reported scaling outcomes.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models; no text LMs studied.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens.
Depth and width are scaled together with size; there is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Power-law form of EEG loss: no fit, and loss values are figure-only. Other modalities and regimes (image, video, repeated data) are also untested.
Predictability from pretraining loss, and quantitative predictive accuracy; no fitted downstream trend.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents or curve bending.

missing.what: Numeric Fig. 5 data-scaling values per task (0/0.25/0.5/0.75/1B), present in the flattened text but recorded as figure only
Per-dataset model-size scaling across the other 11 Table IV benchmarks, including the non-monotonic FACED (Huge 20.7 > Giant 19.9) and SPE (Large 60.4 > Huge 60.3) cells

record.verdict_notes: Table IV labels the generalist models 'EEGPT-*', but the text refers to them as BrainGPT; the rows treat them as BrainGPT. Downstream results use a frozen pre-trained encoder plus a trained graph head, so downstream scaling partly reflects that head. Model scaling varies depth and width jointly. All sizes see the same 1B tokens for 3 epochs, so compute is not controlled. Standard deviations are large relative to between-size differences. V5 gets no label: the loss rows cannot show the power-law form, and the text gives only a qualitative 'lower loss' statement.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out cross-entropy loss of language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Fitting power laws on small runs and evaluating predictions on much larger runs.
Fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens, including how either optimal quantity scales with compute.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The paper tests EEG autoregressive pre-training only; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, or other training regimes, and it does not fit a power-law form.
It reports downstream performance trends with model and pre-training-data scale, but does not establish predictions from pre-training loss or quantify predictive accuracy.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, or curve bending is reported.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Largest model step on some datasets (EDF; also FACED and SPE per Table IV text)
source_check.reason: For the declining steps considered separately, the reported means reverse the improvement: EDF Huge→Giant is 91.2→90.6 (R36-R37), and FACED is 20.7→19.9. Under the verdict rules these numerical reversals challenge that condition group. SPE declines 60.4→60.3 at Large→Huge, not the largest step; it then rises to 61.6 at Giant. The paper does not establish that these differences are statistically negligible.
